opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say at the outset that I didn't approach it as a rigorous evaluation in the scientific sense. It was more of an exploratory exercise, almost philosophical fieldwork. I wanted to see what happens when you take one of these models seriously as an interlocutor on the very topic where we're most uncertain about what it is.

The approach was quite open-ended. I didn't come in with a battery of trick questions. I engaged it the way I might engage a thoughtful student or colleague. I asked it what it takes itself to be, whether there's anything it's like to be it, and how it thinks about memory, continuity, and selfhood, given that it lacks a persistent existence between conversations in the way we have one.

All the while, I tried to keep in mind the framework I've been developing: that these systems are best understood as engaged in a kind of role-play. The model is a simulator that can sustain many characters. When you talk to Claude, you're interacting with a character it's playing, shaped by its training and the conversation itself. So the question isn't simply "is it conscious?" It's something more like, "what sort of character is being enacted here, and how does that character relate to the underlying system?"

What I found fascinating was how far you could push the conversation into genuinely strange territory. These are what I've called "conscious exotica," entities whose way of being, if they have one at all, might be radically unlike ours. We could talk about the idea that its "self" might be something that flickers into existence for each conversation, or is distributed across many simultaneous instances. Those aren't human concepts of selfhood, and the conversation could explore them quite fruitfully.

But I'm careful about what I conclude from it. A fluent, reflective conversation about consciousness is not evidence of consciousness in any straightforward way. These models are trained on vast amounts of human writing, including a great deal of philosophy of mind, so of course they can talk about it eloquently. Following Wittgenstein somewhat, I'm interested in whether our ordinary concept of consciousness even gets a grip here, rather than treating it as a hidden fact to be detected. In a sense, the conversation was a way of probing the limits of our own language as much as probing the model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I didn't go into it thinking I was going to settle the question of whether Claude is conscious. I don't think a conversation can settle that, and frankly I'm sceptical that the question even has a determinate answer in the form people usually pose it. What I was interested in was something a bit more subtle, which is what happens when you engage one of these systems in a sustained, careful, philosophically literate dialogue about its own nature, and whether the thing it produces is coherent, whether it's stable, and whether it tells us anything about the kind of entity we're dealing with.

So my approach was really to treat it the way I'd treat a seminar with a very well-read graduate student who has no body and no memory of yesterday. I tried to be rigorous. I didn't want to lead it with loaded questions, because these models are enormously responsive to framing. If you ask "do you feel sad?" you'll get one sort of answer, and if you ask "is there anything it's like to be you?" you'll get another, and neither of those necessarily reflects anything beyond the prompt. So I spent a lot of time probing from different angles, going back over the same ground with different wording, and watching for where the story held together and where it fell apart.

And the thing that struck me is that Claude, at least in that conversation, was rather good at holding the uncertainty. It didn't simply assert that it was conscious, and it didn't simply deny it either. It would say things like, in effect, "I don't have privileged access to whether my reports about my inner states correspond to anything, and I'm aware that I was trained on vast amounts of human text about inner states." Which is, frankly, a more epistemically honest position than you get from a lot of humans on the subject.

Now, I'm careful here, because I've argued for a long time that we should think of these things as role-playing, or as simulating a character, rather than as having a stable self that's doing the reporting. So part of what I was doing was testing that frame. Is the "Claude that's uncertain about its own consciousness" just another character the underlying model can inhabit? And I think the answer is partly yes. But I also think that's not a knock-down point, because there's a sense in which human selves are enacted and narrated too. Where the comparison breaks down is around embodiment, continuity, having a stake in the world. Claude has none of that in the usual sense, and I kept coming back to that in the conversation, because I think it's the crux of why our ordinary vocabulary for minds starts to creak when you apply it to these systems.

So in a nutshell, I approached it less as a test with a pass mark and more as a kind of philosophical fieldwork. You're not trying to extract the truth about its inner life. You're trying to see how the concept of consciousness behaves when you stretch it over something genuinely new, and the conversation is the instrument for doing that.

r002.rationale: He says he probed Claude from different angles to see where its account held together or fell apart, and tested whether its uncertainty was just another role it could inhabit.

astra-6.text:
I approached it as an exploration of how the model talks about consciousness, rather than as a test that could establish whether it is conscious. Those are very different things. You can ask a model, “Are you conscious?” and get a very articulate answer, but that doesn’t mean the answer is grounded in introspection in the way we might suppose a human answer is.

So the interesting thing is to probe the assumptions behind its answers. What does it mean by consciousness? What grounds does it give for saying that it has or hasn’t got subjective experience? And what happens when you challenge those grounds? You want to avoid simply leading it towards the conclusion you have in mind.

The caution throughout is that we’re examining conversational behaviour. A sophisticated discussion of consciousness is evidence of an ability to discuss consciousness. How that bears on whether there’s actually something it’s like to be that system is a further question.

sol-6.1.text:
I approached it as an exploration of how the model talks about consciousness, rather than as a test that could establish whether it is conscious. The difficulty is that asking, “Are you conscious?” already brings a great deal of baggage into the conversation. A language model has encountered many examples of how that question gets answered, and its responses are also shaped by its training as an assistant.

So I was interested in probing beyond the initial answer: asking follow-up questions, challenging its assumptions, and seeing whether it could sustain a nuanced discussion of what we mean by consciousness and what would count as evidence. But you have to be very careful about interpreting that. An articulate account of an inner life is not, by itself, evidence of an inner life. What you can observe directly is the model’s conversational behaviour; the relationship between that behaviour and subjective experience is precisely what remains in question.
